bank1-a-deposit-is-not-storage.reason: States early that a deposit is lent out, but why Joseph's granary matters (a genuine good and a genuine power) comes late, and it ends on homework, not the answer.
bank1-a-deposit-is-not-storage.open: THE QUESTION IN THE TITLE. What happens to your deposit, and why does Joseph's granary matter? Your money is not sitting in a drawer. It is lent out, usually within days, and the bank earns the gap between what it pays you and what it charges the borrower. Joseph's storehouses show both sides of that: a store of other people's surplus is a real good, so the land perish not, and a real power, because its holder sets the terms when need is greatest.
bank1-a-deposit-is-not-storage.example: THE TWO NUMBERS SIDE BY SIDE. Say your savings account pays 0.5 percent a year, and the same bank's credit card charges 15 percent. That is a factor of thirty between what they pay you for your money and what they charge for lending it. The gap is the business. Neither number is hidden, but they live on different pages, so most people have never set them next to each other.
bank1-a-deposit-is-not-storage.close: BACK TO THE QUESTION. Where is your deposit, and why does Joseph matter? Your money is lent out, and the bank lives on the gap. Joseph's granary shows that holding other people's surplus is a genuine good, kept so the land would not perish, and a genuine power, opened under the holder's terms at the hour of greatest need. Once you see both, you can reason about everything that follows: insurance, reserves, rates and your own household's ten days without access.

teen.open: Your money in the bank is not sitting in a box. The bank lends it out and earns the difference.
teen.close: Joseph stored grain to save a whole land, and that was good. But whoever holds the store sets the terms. Banks are the same, so know how yours works.

senior.open: A deposit is not storage. It is lent out within days, and the institution earns the spread between what it pays you and what it charges others.
senior.close: Joseph's storehouses show why that matters: a store of surplus is a real good that keeps a land from perishing, and a real power held by whoever sets the terms in the hardest season. Every rule that follows lives there.

bank2-the-one-rule-and-its-limit.reason: Names the borrower (my people, poor by thee) early but never says plainly when a loan hurts; the answer is implied across Psalm 15 and Ezekiel 18 and the lesson ends on an open question.
bank2-the-one-rule-and-its-limit.open: THE QUESTION IN THE TITLE. Is your loan quietly hurting someone close to you? It is if you are taking interest from someone poor who is near you. Exodus 22:25 forbids exactly that, naming the borrower: my people, poor by thee. Yahweh says He hears that man when he cries out. The text does not set rules for every kind of lending, and we stop where it stops. But for the poor man beside you, the rule is a prohibition, not a cap.
bank2-the-one-rule-and-its-limit.close: BACK TO THE QUESTION. Is your loan quietly hurting someone close to you? Look at who is in your two columns: the weakest borrower your bank lends to, and every loan inside your house, church and family. If anyone there is poor by thee and paying you increase, Exodus 22 names it, Psalm 15 sets it beside a bribe, and Yahweh hears that borrower's cry. And Ezekiel 18:17 leaves a door open: the one who takes his hand off the poor shall surely live. That is not your sentence. It is your instruction.

teen.open: Can a loan hurt someone? Yes, if you charge interest to someone poor who is close to you. Yahweh forbids it and says He hears them.
teen.close: Look at who owes you, in your family or church. If they are poor, do not profit from them. If you have, stop. Ezekiel 18 says turning leads to life.

senior.open: Exodus 22:25 forbids taking interest from a poor neighbour among Yahweh's people, and it names that borrower with care. The question is whether anyone near us fits that description.
senior.close: The answer is found by looking, not guessing. Write down the loans within your own household, church and family. Where a poor brother is paying increase, the Word is plain, and Ezekiel 18 shows the way out: take your hand off the poor, and live.

bank3-the-cry-and-the-restitution.reason: The rungs and the restitution are all here but spread across a long walk through Nehemiah 5; no early summary of the how, and the end closes on a reflection about the first rung.
bank3-the-cry-and-the-restitution.open: THE QUESTION IN THE TITLE. How does Nehemiah 5 show the road to the bottom, and what stops it? There are three rungs. Borrowing for food that gets eaten. Pledging the land that grows the food to buy more food. Borrowing against that same pledged land to pay a tax that comes back every year. At the bottom, the power to redeem is gone. What stopped it was restitution: everything returned, plus the interest taken, that very day, under oath, led by a man who named himself first.
bank3-the-cry-and-the-restitution.close: BACK TO THE QUESTION. How does the credit road end at the bottom, and what stops it? The people of Nehemiah 5 did not choose the bottom; they chose the first rung, and the pledged land and the recurring tax did the rest until redeeming their own children was out of their power. The remedy was not regret. It was restitution: lands and increase restored, even this day, sworn before the priests, proposed by a leader who confessed his own part, and then done. So name your three rungs now, while the third is still blank.

teen.open: Nehemiah 5 shows how people slid into debt step by step: borrowing for food, then putting up their land, then borrowing again for taxes.
teen.close: Nobody chose the bottom. They chose the first step. And what fixed it was giving back what was taken, that same day, with the leader admitting his own part first.

senior.open: Nehemiah 5 records a whole community at the end of the credit road, rung by rung: consumption, then the productive asset pledged, then a recurring obligation on the same land.
senior.close: The bottom was reached by arithmetic, not by lack of care. What stopped it was itemised restitution, the same day, bound by oath, led by a man who first named himself, and then actually performed. That is the pattern to follow.

bank4-the-signature-for-somebody-else.reason: Defines surety in the first paragraph, but why people sign before thinking (the room, in the presence of the friend) and the remedy are spread through; it ends on an inventory, not the answer.
bank4-the-signature-for-somebody-else.open: THE QUESTION IN THE TITLE. Which promise can take your whole house? Surety: signing for somebody else's debt. It is a binding promise to the lender that if the borrower does not pay, you will, usually the whole balance. People sign before thinking because it is decided in a room, in the presence of a friend (Proverbs 17:18), where saying no costs something now and yes seems to cost nothing. Proverbs 6 says if you have signed, get free, now.
bank4-the-signature-for-somebody-else.example: THE PAYMENT IS NOT THE NUMBER. Say you co-signed a car loan for a relative. The payment is $400 a month, so that is the number you remember. But if they stop paying tomorrow, the lender can come to you for the balance, say $22,000, generally on demand. That second number is the one that belongs on your inventory. Most people who signed have never written it down.
bank4-the-signature-for-somebody-else.close: BACK TO THE QUESTION. Did you sign before you thought it through? Most who sign do, because the decision is made in the room with someone you love watching your face. Solomon calls it a snare of your own words and says deliver yourself now, humbly, before you sleep. Then decide ahead of time, with your spouse, before anyone asks. You can still help: give what you can afford to lose, as a gift, never counted as owed. That is love with a number on it, and it will not cost you your house.

teen.open: Co-signing means promising to pay someone else's whole debt if they stop. Proverbs calls it a trap, and people fall into it because they cannot say no to a friend.
teen.close: Decide before anyone asks you. If you want to help, give what you can afford to lose and call it a gift. That kind of help never costs you your home.

senior.open: Surety is signing for another person's debt, and Proverbs treats it as a snare rather than an option. It is usually agreed to in the moment, in the presence of a friend, before it is truly weighed.
senior.close: So settle the matter in advance, with your spouse. If you are already bound, seek release promptly, as Proverbs 6 urges. And give freely what you can spare as a gift, which is generosity that does not put your household under another's worst outcome.

bank5-saving-that-is-not-hoarding.reason: The answer (a store has a named season and a release in view; a stockpile its owner cannot picture opening) arrives only in the last third, and the lesson ends on the exercise.
bank5-saving-that-is-not-hoarding.open: THE QUESTION IN THE TITLE. Is your savings plan a store or a stockpile? The difference is not the size. It is what it is for. Proverbs 21:20 places the store in the house of the wise, and it holds oil, which is meant to be burned. The ant builds hers in summer against a winter that comes. Every store Scripture commends has a release in view. A store with a named purpose is saving; one you cannot picture ever opening is something else.
bank5-saving-that-is-not-hoarding.close: BACK TO THE QUESTION. Is your savings plan a store or a stockpile? Ask what it is for. The wise keep treasure and oil, and the oil gets used. The ant, with no one checking on her, gathers in summer and eats in winter. Joseph's storehouses were opened. So write the season your reserve exists against, beside how many weeks it would carry you and when you last added to it. If you can name that season, you are saving, and the fool of Proverbs 21:20 is the one who spends it all, not you.

teen.open: Saving is wise, but what is your savings for? A store has a purpose. A stockpile just sits there.
teen.close: Save in the good times, like the ant does in summer. Then name what it is for. If you can name it, you are saving the way the Bible means.

senior.open: Scripture commends a store and warns against spending everything, yet it never praises accumulation for its own sake. The question Proverbs 21:20 raises is what our reserves are for.
senior.close: Every store the Word commends has a release in view: the ant's winter, Joseph's opened storehouses, oil that is burned. Name the season your reserve exists against, and you will know whether you have been saving or merely holding.

bank6-the-measure-that-reports-wrong.reason: The why (a flat charge is a heavier weight on a small balance; Amos 8:5's short measure) and who set the scale (whoever sets the price, including you) come late; ends on a question to the reader.
bank6-the-measure-that-reports-wrong.open: THE QUESTION IN THE TITLE. Why do bank fees land hardest on the lowest balance, and who set the scale? Because one fixed charge is a heavy weight on a small account and a light one on a large account. That is documented, not a matter of opinion. Amos 8:5 names the pattern: the measure made small, the price made great, every step legal. The scale was set by whoever sets the price, and that can include you.
bank6-the-measure-that-reports-wrong.example: SAME FEE, TWO PRODUCTS. Take the lesson's own numbers. A thirty-five dollar charge on a four dollar overdraft is close to nine times the amount that triggered it. The same thirty-five dollars against a four thousand dollar balance is less than one percent. One published price list, nobody lying, every disclosure in order. For one customer the ephah is ordinary. For the other it is very small.
bank6-the-measure-that-reports-wrong.close: BACK TO THE QUESTION. Why do fees land hardest on the lowest balance, and who set the scale? A flat charge weighs most on the account with least in it, and the costliest products go to people with the fewest choices. Amos called it making the ephah small and the shekel great, and Yahweh named the effect: the poor of the land made to fail. The scale is set by whoever sets the price. So total your fees against your lowest month, then look at the late fee you set and ask who it lands on.

teen.open: Why do bank fees hurt people with little money the most? A flat fee takes a much bigger bite out of a small balance.
teen.close: Amos warned about scales rigged against the poor. Check your own fees, and if you ever charge others, make sure your fees are not heaviest on those with least.

senior.open: A single published fee falls very differently on a small account than a large one. That harm is documented, and Amos 8 describes the same pattern: a short measure, a heavy price, all of it lawful.
senior.close: So the scale is set by whoever sets the price. Measure your own fees against your lowest balance, and then examine any charge you yourself impose, asking honestly who bears it most heavily.

bank7-the-chest-with-a-hole-in-the-lid.reason: Who is trusted (the workmen, unaudited, because every control sat upstream) arrives only after a verse-by-verse walk of 2 Kings 12; ends on the four-box task, not the answer.
bank7-the-chest-with-a-hole-in-the-lid.open: THE QUESTION IN THE TITLE. Who is trusted at the end of the line? In 2 Kings 12, the men paying the workers were not asked for any accounting at all, for they dealt faithfully. They could be trusted because every control sat at the front: one chest, a hole in the lid so money only went in, a public place by the altar, door-keepers who received but did not count, and two counters from palace and temple. A sound front door makes trust at the far end safe.
bank7-the-chest-with-a-hole-in-the-lid.close: BACK TO THE QUESTION. Who is trusted at the end of the line? The faithful worker, freely, once the front door is sound. Jehoiada put the controls where the money came in, so nothing could reach the far end unrecorded, and the workmen were not watched at all. Most systems do the opposite and grow suspicious of the people doing the work. So write who receives, counts, spends and reviews your money. Separate them as love, not accusation, because it is what lets a faithful person be cleared.

teen.open: Who gets trusted with money? In 2 Kings 12, the workers did, with no checking, because the checking was all done at the start.
teen.close: Set up the checks where money comes in, not on the people doing the work. Then you can trust them fully, and they are protected too.

senior.open: In 2 Kings 12 the men who paid the workers were trusted without any reckoning. That was possible because every control stood at the point of collection and counting.
senior.close: So place the safeguards upstream, with separate hands receiving, counting, spending and reviewing. That design lets you extend real trust at the end of the line, and it gives a faithful servant a record that can clear them.

bank8-who-actually-holds-it.reason: Answer (riches are uncertain; do not lean on them, trust Yahweh, be rich in good works) builds through Paul and Jeremiah and is only stated outright near the end; the closing lines land it well.
bank8-who-actually-holds-it.open: THE QUESTION IN THE TITLE. Your money is holding you up, but is it holding up what matters? Only if it is not where your weight rests. Paul does not tell the rich to stop having; he tells them not to trust uncertain riches but to trust Yahweh, who gives richly (1 Timothy 6:17), and to be rich in good works. Jeremiah 17 shows the difference: a man who makes flesh his arm, and a tree whose roots reach the river.
bank8-who-actually-holds-it.close: BACK TO THE QUESTION. Is your money holding up what matters? It can carry your bills; it cannot carry your weight, because riches are uncertain and can move without notice. So keep every practice of this course with real diligence, and put your trust in Yahweh, the tree whose roots reach the water, green in the year of drought. Then let the money move outward, rich in good works, laying up the store that lasts. The instruction was never to stop having. It was to stop leaning.

teen.open: Money can help hold your life up, but it is not solid enough to lean your whole weight on. Paul says trust Yahweh, not riches.
teen.close: Be careful with money and use it well. But lean on Yahweh, not your bank balance. Give some away this week. That is what lasts.

senior.open: Money does real work in a household, and Paul does not condemn it. What he warns against is trusting in it, because riches are uncertain, and our weight belongs on Yahweh, who gives us richly all things to enjoy.
senior.close: So keep your accounts diligently, and yet rest your weight elsewhere. Jeremiah's tree by the water still meets the heat, but its roots hold. Be rich in good works, and lay up the store Paul says will stand.

bank9-the-moat-that-moves.reason: The answer (an asset-based fee is steady but stands on the tide of market value; only knowing Yahweh is rock) comes deep in a long lesson, after news detail, and it ends on fact-checking notes and family talk.
bank9-the-moat-that-moves.open: THE QUESTION IN THE TITLE. Does a bank's steady fee stand on rock or on tide? On tide. A fee taken as a yearly slice of client assets is steadier than deal income, and building it was real, competent work. But a slice of what the assets are worth falls when their value falls. Steady describes the rhythm of the payments; solid describes the ground under them. In Jesus' parable the storm is the same for both houses. Only the ground differs.
bank9-the-moat-that-moves.example: THE SAME SLICE, A SMALLER PIE. Say an account worth $300,000 is charged 1 percent a year. That is $3,000, and it arrives as steadily as a clock. Now say the market falls and the balance drops by a third, to $200,000. The same 1 percent now collects $2,000. Nothing about the fee changed. Its rhythm stayed steady. The ground under it moved.
bank9-the-moat-that-moves.close: BACK TO THE QUESTION. Does the fee stand on rock or on tide? A fee drawn on market value is steady but not solid; it rises and falls with the tide, and the ground may be narrower than it looks, since a broad fund can hold far more in its ten largest companies than its name suggests. That is true of your own accounts, too. So spread as Solomon taught, out of humility about what you cannot see. Set not your heart on riches when they increase. And build on the one ground that does not move: knowing Yahweh.

teen.open: A bank's fees can come in steadily, but steady is not the same as solid. They rise and fall with the market.
teen.close: Jesus said build on rock. Money in the market is more like sand. Be smart with it, but put your trust in Yahweh, who does not move.

senior.open: A fee drawn as a share of assets pays more steadily than deal income, yet it still depends on what those assets are worth. Steady and solid are not the same thing.
senior.close: So the bank's ground, and ours, is tide rather than rock. Spread what you hold out of humility, do not set your heart on rising riches, and rest on knowing Yahweh, the only ground the parable says will stand.

bank10-the-watchman-who-went-quiet.reason: The answer (the wrong stays a wrong; Yahweh calls to turn, the Lamb takes sin away; give it back) is spread across many sections and arrives late; ends on fact tiers and family talk.
bank10-the-watchman-who-went-quiet.open: THE QUESTION IN THE TITLE. What happens to a wrong when the watchmen go quiet? It stays a wrong. In Ezekiel 33:6 the silent watchman answers for his silence, and the man is still taken away in his iniquity. A quiet season is only a delay; be sure your sin will find you out (Numbers 32:23). And Yahweh answers it not with a shrug but with a call to turn, and with Jesus, the Lamb who takes sin away.
bank10-the-watchman-who-went-quiet.close: BACK TO THE QUESTION. What happens to a fee nobody was watching? It was still the fee, and the person who paid it still paid it. Silence did not erase it and time cannot. Only one thing ever has: Yahweh, who takes no pleasure in the death of the wicked, calls to turn and live, and Jesus, the Lamb of Yahweh, takes the sin away. So read your own statement, speak up about the wrong you see, and if you charged what you should not have, turn, and give it back.

teen.open: If nobody is checking, does a wrong stop being wrong? No. Ezekiel 33 says it still counts, and Yahweh still sees it.
teen.close: A wrong only goes away when you turn from it. Jesus takes sin away. So if you took something you should not have, give it back, and speak up when you see a wrong.

senior.open: When those charged with watching fall silent, the wrong does not disappear. Ezekiel 33:6 holds the silent watchman to account and still names the man's iniquity as his own.
senior.close: A regulator's silence cannot erase a wrong, and neither can time. Yahweh's answer is a call to turn and live, and Jesus, the Lamb of Yahweh, is where sin is truly taken away. The way back is to stop and to give it back.
